newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn's gold plan not to impact inflation-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's gold plan not to impact inflation-analysts.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue gold reserves in a bid to shore up public finances should be largely neutral for money supply growth, keeping inflationary pressures in check, analysts said Friday.

"Under normal circumstances the transfer of a portion of central bank profits to the government does not impact money supply growth in any negative fashion," said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
Economists agreed that the Bundesbank would sign off on a plan to unlock hidden reserves only on the condition it did not upset its carefully watched money supply targets.

M3 money supply, including cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits, is generally seen as a leading indicator for inflation, which the Bundesbank tries to keep under two percent in the medium-term.

Arguing the change would occur largely on paper, Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber in London said, "If (Bonn's plan) did increase money supply, then the Bundesbank surely would not agree to it."
She added that the Bundesbank, which is known to oppose gold sales to cover budgetary shortfalls, likely drove this point home to Waigel on Thursday.
"I think if Waigel had wanted to sell gold, (Bundesbank president) Hans Tietmeyer would not have let him out of the room alive," she said.
Traditionally the Bundesbank transfers a portion of its profit to the government which uses it to retire old debt.

A higher transfer would be booked as extraordinary earnings which Bonn plans to funnel into the government's inherited debt repayment fund. This would then be booked as a net profit which push back the government's deficit, helping Bonn come one step closer to meeting the Maastricht Treaty deficit criterion.

And while a transfer of a bigger Bundesbank profit could be seen to spur money supply growth, analysts noted the central bank would quickly neutralise whatever expansionary impact a bigger transfer might have.
"The Bundesbank will immediately neutralise the amount that Bonn may receive," Ralf Kugelstadt, economist at UBS in Frankfurt said.
While economists remain in the dark about how large the future transfers might be, they agreed the Bundesbank had plenty of tools to drain excess liqudity.
"Even if they cannot take care of the neutralisation at the weekly repo, they could do swaps or an number of other things to equalise liquidity," Fels said.
In April, Bonn received 8.83 billion marks from the Bundesbank's 1996 annual profits which was below the 10.32 billion marks the government received for 1995.
If Bonn's plans to ask for a payout on half of 1997's profits this year are approved, Fels said the government could receive around 10 billion marks this year. "And it would be higher next year."
Reasons for economists' uncertainty about the transfer is that no more details have been announced after the basic plan was outlined on Thursday.

While the Bundesbank's gold reserves are currently valued at 13.69 billion marks and the market value would be above 50 billion marks, economists said it would be unusual for the stock to be revalued to exactly market levels.
Even the Bundesbank declined further comment on technical issues, saying it had no further details.
